Listen to this article Share At one point, Frank Aigbogun wanted to stop being a journalist. After 14 years at Vanguard, where he had risen from pioneer news editor to editor of all its titles, he was ready to try something different. He wanted to manufacture plastic products. An avid collector of plastics, he believed there was an opportunity to build a small factory around the products he had come to appreciate. He began looking for investors and trying to raise the capital to get the business started, but the funding proved difficult to secure. The plan gradually lost momentum, and Aigbogun found himself turning back to the profession he had spent much of his adult life building a career in. The first person he approached about starting a newspaper business was Pat Utomi, a professor of political economy. On a Sunday, Aigbogun visited Utomi at his residence in Ikoyi, Lagos, to discuss the idea and work through what such an undertaking might require. He took notes during their conversation, and more than two decades later, he still has them. Utomi would eventually become the first chairman of BusinessDay, the newspaper Aigbogun went on to establish. Read also: tinubu-hails-frank-aigbogun-businessday-publisher-for-commitment-to-responsible-journalism-at-70 It is an unusual route into the story of a man who turnes 70 on November 1, 2026, and whose name has become closely associated with business journalism in Nigeria. But the plastic factory plan reveals something important about Aigbogun: his career was not simply the result of a lifelong determination to own a newspaper. It was shaped by experience, curiosity, failed plans and a willingness to return to what he knew when another ambition did not work out. That willingness to learn had begun long before BusinessDay. Born on November 1, 1956, Aigbogun grew up in Sapele, Delta State, in circumstances he describes without romanticising them. He did not have much, but he learnt early to make something of what was available. “I had nothing, so for me anything was something,” he has said. It is a simple recollection, but it offers a glimpse of the outlook that would follow him through a career in which he repeatedly had to build with limited resources and persuade others to believe in an idea. After studying Mass Communication at the Institute of Management and Technology, Enugu, he began his journalism career at The Guardian in Lagos in 1982, before the newspaper had started publishing. His first assignment was not the reporting job many young journalists might have expected. He was asked to prepare a training manual for journalists who would be recruited into the new organisation. His early career also took him away from Lagos. He was posted to the office of the chief press secretary to Abubakar Rimi, then governor of Kano State, where he worked with Sule Abuze. With the help of The Guardian, he was transferred from Kano to Wudil. After an orientation there, he eventually returned to Lagos, arriving on October 20, 1982, according to his account. Read also: ngx-group-ceo-felicitates-with-frank-aigbogun-at-70 At The Guardian, he rose quickly, eventually heading the reportorial corps for the Sunday Guardian. But he was conscious that becoming a good journalist required more than completing assignments and meeting deadlines. He regularly visited the United States Information Service library at Race Course in Lagos, reading and studying to improve his writing and understanding of the profession. The habit reflected an approach he would later describe in straightforward terms: he was a learner who listened, observed and asked questions. That instinct stayed with him when he joined Vanguard as a pioneer news editor. He later became deputy editor and then editor of all the newspaper’s titles, spending 14 years at the organisation. It was a formative period, not only because of the positions he held, but because it gave him a close view of what it took to produce a newspaper every day and sustain a newsroom over time. Under his editorial leadership, Vanguard’s daily circulation reached 300,000 copies. He learnt from the people who built the newspaper and from a publisher who believed in journalism. The experience gave him an understanding of the relationship between editorial ambition and the practical demands of running a media organisation. It also prepared him for a different kind of journalism when he moved on from Vanguard. Aigbogun subsequently worked with the Associated Press, first as a freelancer and later as its Lagos correspondent for 11 years. The international news agency exposed him to a different scale of reporting and showed him what journalism could achieve when reporters had the resources to investigate, travel and pursue stories beyond the immediate demands of the daily news cycle. Two assignments stand out in his recollection. One was the death of former military ruler Sani Abacha. The other was the explosion at the Jesse oil pipeline near his hometown of Sapele, where about 200 people died. The tragedy was particularly disturbing because a US company extinguishing the fire burning the Nigerians caught in the disaster. Aigbogun broke the story for the Associated Press and received an award for his reporting. The Jesse story carried a personal weight because it happened close to where he grew up, but it also demonstrated the value of reporting that went beyond the immediate account of an incident. The presence of a foreign company putting out a fire that had consumed Nigerian lives was an important part of the story. It was the kind of detail that could be missed if a reporter simply recorded the explosion and the casualties. By the time he began considering his next move, Aigbogun had experienced journalism from several sides: the early work of establishing a newspaper, the pressure of running a busy newsroom and the demands of reporting for an international agency. Those experiences would become important when he returned to the idea of building a media organisation of his own. BusinessDay was officially launched on July 2, 2001. It began as a weekly publication, but Aigbogun’s intention had always been to produce a newspaper every business day. The name itself reflected that ambition. The challenge was persuading readers to embrace a daily business newspaper in a market where established publications already competed for attention and where the idea of a specialised daily title was still unfamiliar. The transition from a weekly publication to a daily newspaper required substantial investment. It also required patience. Readers did not immediately respond in the numbers the founders had hoped for, and copies went unsold. But Aigbogun was not prepared to abandon the idea simply because the market was slow to accept it. The company had shareholders willing to support the undertaking, and the newspaper continued to work towards the daily publishing model he had envisaged from the beginning. Building BusinessDay also meant learning that editorial quality alone could not guarantee the survival of a media company. For Aigbogun, the commercial side of journalism was never separate from the newsroom’s ability to do its work. He puts the relationship plainly: “In media business, as you focus on the content side, if the commercial side is weak, the content side will weaken and possibly collapse.” It is a lesson that has informed his view of journalism and the responsibilities of those who lead media organisations. Journalists, he argues, should be able to take on roles across the value chain, rather than regard the newsroom as the only part of the business that matters. They need to understand how their organisations earn revenue, manage costs and remain sustainable, because the quality of journalism depends in part on whether the institution producing it can survive. His own approach to management has been shaped by a willingness to learn from people around him. “I am a very good learner and I listen a lot,” he says, pointing to the importance of asking questions. Having worked in different newsrooms and seen different models of journalism, he understood that leadership was not simply about issuing instructions. It required understanding people, recognising their strengths and being prepared to learn from them. That outlook has become particularly relevant as the business of journalism has changed. Newspapers no longer enjoy the control they once had over what audiences read, and the growth of digital platforms has altered how people discover, consume and pay for information. Aigbogun remembers a period when newspaper circulation could exceed one million copies and readers queued to buy the day’s papers. The industry cannot assume that those habits will return. “If the media knows that it should be running every day it wakes up, we will be at a better place by today,” he has said, reflecting on the need for publishers to treat their organisations as businesses that must continually adapt. He has also argued that media companies need to move away from an overwhelming dependence on advertising and build stronger relationships with readers who are willing to pay for content. In his view, reader revenue should account for at least 40 percent of a media organisation’s income if the business is to be stable. But adaptation, for him, is not simply about adopting new technology or finding another source of revenue. It is also about understanding the people journalism is meant to serve. “It is important for journalism to recreate itself, to continue to create a connection with society, create something local and of interest to the people and be sure whatever it does resonates with the people,” he says. That emphasis on relevance is consistent with a view he expressed years ago about the limitations of Nigerian newspaper coverage. In a 2005 reflection, he observed that newspapers were highly efficient at communicating everyday government information, while leaving large parts of the country’s social life uncovered. The challenge, then and now, is to report beyond the familiar institutions and official voices, and to pay attention to the experiences of people whose lives rarely make it into the news. Aigbogun’s public responsibilities have extended beyond BusinessDay. He has served as president of the Lagos Business School Alumni Association and was appointed chairman of the Impact Investors Foundation in January 2025. He is also vice-chair of the advisory board of the National Advisory Board for Impact Investing. In April 2025, he was elected chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Institute of Management and Technology Alumni Association in Enugu. His other public roles have included serving on the board of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group and participating in the Vision 2010 committee, where he was alternate rapporteur of the subcommittee on competition and deregulation. In 2024, he received the Diamond Awards for Media Excellence Lifetime Achievement Award. For all the positions and responsibilities, however, Aigbogun speaks about life in terms that are less concerned with titles than with choices. “In life, you must choose your battles. Don’t be known for everything. Just choose a few things you want to do and do well,” he says. It is a philosophy that appears to have guided both his professional decisions and the way he approaches the demands placed on him. He describes himself as someone who tries to remain positive, and whose response to setbacks is captured in the phrase, “Never say never.” His faith is another source of strength. “I have learnt to believe in God, my God, the Almighty God,” he says, describing that belief as an inner strength that has carried him through life. Asked what he would like to do for the rest of his life, he speaks of wanting to know God more and deepen that understanding. Away from work, he is an avid reader and a staunch Manchester United supporter. He is married to Juliet Aigbogun, and they have three children. These parts of his life sit alongside the demands of running a media organisation, but they also help explain the interests and convictions that have remained with him outside the newsroom. At 70, Aigbogun is thinking less about starting another institution than about ensuring that what he has built can endure. He describes the next phase as a period of consolidation and of closing the loop, with attention to creating stronger foundations for both his personal life and BusinessDay. It is not simply a question of handing over responsibility; he wants to leave behind an organisation that is sufficiently sound to continue beyond his own leadership. “It is time for me to bring together what I have been doing, so that when it is time to hand over, it is something complete, alive and solid,” he says. The ambition is telling. The man who once considered leaving journalism to make plastic products has spent much of his life building a newspaper, learning the business behind it and arguing that journalism must keep changing if it is to remain useful. At 70, his attention is on what comes after him: not just the name of an institution, but whether the institution is strong enough to keep doing the work.
